<form class="book-practice" id="quiz-p05" data-practice-set="P05" novalidate>
<p id="quiz-p05-instructions">Choose one answer for each of the 10 questions. Complete the set, then select <strong>Check answers</strong> to see your score and explanations. Each question is worth one point.</p>
<noscript><p>For a self-check without JavaScript, record your choices, then open the answer key below.</p></noscript>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p05-01" aria-describedby="quiz-p05-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">1.</span> A client accurately summarizes a proposal but declines it. What should the adviser investigate before preparing another explanation?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-01-a"><input type="radio" id="p05-01-a" name="p05-01" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Which communication channel would make the same explanation more familiar</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-01-b"><input type="radio" id="p05-01-b" name="p05-01" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Which technical terms need a simpler definition</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-01-c"><input type="radio" id="p05-01-c" name="p05-01" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Which visual layout would make the summary easier to scan</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-01-d"><input type="radio" id="p05-01-d" name="p05-01" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Which consequences conflict with the client&#x27;s priorities</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-01-e"><input type="radio" id="p05-01-e" name="p05-01" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Which section should be repeated more prominently</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p05-01-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p05-02" aria-describedby="quiz-p05-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">2.</span> A presentation opens with a moving patient story and claims that similar patients usually recover after the treatment. Which evidence best supports the frequency claim?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-02-a"><input type="radio" id="p05-02-a" name="p05-02" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> The number of favorable treatment stories reported in the local press</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-02-b"><input type="radio" id="p05-02-b" name="p05-02" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Clinicians&#x27; recollections of the cases they found most striking</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-02-c"><input type="radio" id="p05-02-c" name="p05-02" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Follow-up outcomes from a representative sample of comparable patients</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-02-d"><input type="radio" id="p05-02-d" name="p05-02" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Satisfaction ratings from patients who completed the full treatment</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-02-e"><input type="radio" id="p05-02-e" name="p05-02" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Detailed accounts from several patients selected for successful recovery</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p05-02-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p05-03" aria-describedby="quiz-p05-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">3.</span> A manager says a pilot is optional but uses a threatening tone and implies refusal will be remembered. Which redesign best preserves meaningful choice?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-03-a"><input type="radio" id="p05-03-a" name="p05-03" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Replace the threatening words while preserving the penalty.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-03-b"><input type="radio" id="p05-03-b" name="p05-03" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Keep the implied penalty but add the word voluntary twice.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-03-c"><input type="radio" id="p05-03-c" name="p05-03" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Count quiet agreement as informed acceptance.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-03-d"><input type="radio" id="p05-03-d" name="p05-03" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Remove refusal penalties and explain the options without pressure.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-03-e"><input type="radio" id="p05-03-e" name="p05-03" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Offer more promotional stories without explaining refusal.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p05-03-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p05-04" aria-describedby="quiz-p05-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">4.</span> A story increases sympathy for a proposal&#x27;s beneficiary, but the audience still worries about funding. What is the most useful next step?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-04-a"><input type="radio" id="p05-04-a" name="p05-04" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Treat sympathy as proof that the funding plan is feasible.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-04-b"><input type="radio" id="p05-04-b" name="p05-04" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Repeat the story until the funding question is no longer raised.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-04-c"><input type="radio" id="p05-04-c" name="p05-04" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Address the funding concern with evidence while retaining the story&#x27;s concrete perspective.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-04-d"><input type="radio" id="p05-04-d" name="p05-04" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Label the question a lack of empathy.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-04-e"><input type="radio" id="p05-04-e" name="p05-04" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Omit all cost information to preserve the story&#x27;s impact.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p05-04-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p05-05" aria-describedby="quiz-p05-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">5.</span> A colleague says a schedule change made her feel disregarded. Which response best checks understanding before proposing a fix?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-05-a"><input type="radio" id="p05-05-a" name="p05-05" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> “The schedule is efficient, so there is no problem.”</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-05-b"><input type="radio" id="p05-05-b" name="p05-05" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> “I know exactly how you feel, so let us move on.”</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-05-c"><input type="radio" id="p05-05-c" name="p05-05" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> “You should use the calendar more carefully.”</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-05-d"><input type="radio" id="p05-05-d" name="p05-05" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> “Everyone feels that way about schedules.”</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-05-e"><input type="radio" id="p05-05-e" name="p05-05" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> “Was being excluded the main concern, or have I misunderstood?”</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p05-05-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p05-06" aria-describedby="quiz-p05-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">6.</span> A policy brief recommends expanding a service. The expansion is worthwhile at high demand but costly at low demand, and future demand is uncertain. Which addition would best help readers assess the recommendation?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-06-a"><input type="radio" id="p05-06-a" name="p05-06" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> A comprehensive list of forecasting difficulties arranged by data source</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-06-b"><input type="radio" id="p05-06-b" name="p05-06" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> A demand range and the level at which expansion ceases to be worthwhile</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-06-c"><input type="radio" id="p05-06-c" name="p05-06" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> A general limitations paragraph noting that future conditions may change</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-06-d"><input type="radio" id="p05-06-d" name="p05-06" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> A precise central demand estimate accompanied by the authors&#x27; confidence rating</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-06-e"><input type="radio" id="p05-06-e" name="p05-06" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> A successful expansion elsewhere with a similar estimated average demand</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p05-06-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p05-07" aria-describedby="quiz-p05-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">7.</span> A message earns higher credibility ratings in a randomized study. The team is considering using it to increase completed vaccinations. Which follow-up would best test that objective?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-07-a"><input type="radio" id="p05-07-a" name="p05-07" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Compare how accurately recipients remember the messages after a week.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-07-b"><input type="radio" id="p05-07-b" name="p05-07" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Ask a larger sample how likely they would be to share each message.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-07-c"><input type="radio" id="p05-07-c" name="p05-07" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Repeat the study with a more detailed scale measuring the message&#x27;s credibility.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-07-d"><input type="radio" id="p05-07-d" name="p05-07" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Compare recipients&#x27; ratings of the medical expertise conveyed by each message.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-07-e"><input type="radio" id="p05-07-e" name="p05-07" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Randomly assign the messages in the intended setting and compare completed vaccinations.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p05-07-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p05-08" aria-describedby="quiz-p05-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">8.</span> After publicly blaming a colleague for a missed handoff, a manager discovers that an omitted instruction caused the problem. Which response most directly repairs the harm from the accusation?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-08-a"><input type="radio" id="p05-08-a" name="p05-08" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Ask the team to stop discussing the incident and focus on the next delivery.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-08-b"><input type="radio" id="p05-08-b" name="p05-08" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Privately send the missing instruction and agree on the next handoff date.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-08-c"><input type="radio" id="p05-08-c" name="p05-08" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Explain privately why the available information originally suggested the colleague was at fault.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-08-d"><input type="radio" id="p05-08-d" name="p05-08" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Correct the account before the same audience and acknowledge the colleague&#x27;s treatment.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-08-e"><input type="radio" id="p05-08-e" name="p05-08" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Introduce a checklist that prevents similar omissions in future handoffs.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p05-08-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p05-09" aria-describedby="quiz-p05-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">9.</span> A training advertisement features a top performer whose income doubled after attending. There is no comparison group, and attendees selected themselves. Which revised claim best fits the evidence?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-09-a"><input type="radio" id="p05-09-a" name="p05-09" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Income doubled afterward; the training&#x27;s causal contribution remains unknown.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-09-b"><input type="radio" id="p05-09-b" name="p05-09" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Training caused this person&#x27;s full income increase.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-09-c"><input type="radio" id="p05-09-c" name="p05-09" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Self-selection proves that the training had zero effect.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-09-d"><input type="radio" id="p05-09-d" name="p05-09" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Training doubled income for a typical attendee.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-09-e"><input type="radio" id="p05-09-e" name="p05-09" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> The case establishes the expected gain for a new applicant.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p05-09-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p05-10" aria-describedby="quiz-p05-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">10.</span> A workflow pilot succeeds on routine cases, but staff report that unusual cases require exceptions the system blocks. A manager proposes a more persuasive presentation before expanding the pilot. Which alternative best tests the substance of the objection?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-10-a"><input type="radio" id="p05-10-a" name="p05-10" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Give staff a simpler explanation of why consistent procedures improve performance.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-10-b"><input type="radio" id="p05-10-b" name="p05-10" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Collect more favorable evaluations from staff who mainly handle routine cases.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-10-c"><input type="radio" id="p05-10-c" name="p05-10" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Have the pilot&#x27;s strongest advocates demonstrate the routine cases to another team.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-10-d"><input type="radio" id="p05-10-d" name="p05-10" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Agree on an exception procedure with staff and test it on the unusual cases.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p05-10-e"><input type="radio" id="p05-10-e" name="p05-10" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Ask an external expert to endorse the workflow before the next implementation meeting.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p05-10-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<div class="practice-controls"><p class="practice-progress" aria-live="polite">0 of 10 answered</p>
<button class="practice-submit" type="submit" disabled>Check answers</button>
<button class="practice-retry" type="button" hidden>Try again</button></div>
<p class="practice-score" role="status" tabindex="-1" hidden></p>
<details class="practice-key" id="answers-p05"><summary>Answers and explanations</summary><ol class="practice-answer-list">
<li data-answer="3" data-question="p05-01"><h3>Question 1: D</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Which communication channel would make the same explanation more familiar <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Familiarity with a channel does not identify the client&#x27;s substantive objection.</dd>
<dt>B. Which technical terms need a simpler definition <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This targets a comprehension problem despite the accurate summary.</dd>
<dt>C. Which visual layout would make the summary easier to scan <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Improved presentation does not directly investigate why an understood proposal was rejected.</dd>
<dt>D. Which consequences conflict with the client&#x27;s priorities <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Accurate understanding leaves open substantive disagreement about the proposal&#x27;s value to the client.</dd>
<dt>E. Which section should be repeated more prominently <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Repetition need not resolve disagreement about consequences.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/30-persuasion.html">Chapter 30</a> · <a href="../chapters/33-communication.html">Chapter 33</a>. <a href="#p05-01">Back to question 1</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="2" data-question="p05-02"><h3>Question 2: C</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. The number of favorable treatment stories reported in the local press <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Media selection and an absent patient denominator prevent a recovery-rate estimate.</dd>
<dt>B. Clinicians&#x27; recollections of the cases they found most striking <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Memorable cases can be unrepresentative of the patients treated.</dd>
<dt>C. Follow-up outcomes from a representative sample of comparable patients <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>An appropriate sample with outcome follow-up supports an estimate of how frequently recovery occurs; it does not by itself establish a treatment effect.</dd>
<dt>D. Satisfaction ratings from patients who completed the full treatment <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Satisfaction among completers is neither recovery frequency nor a representative outcome measure for all comparable patients.</dd>
<dt>E. Detailed accounts from several patients selected for successful recovery <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Selected successes do not provide the denominator needed to estimate a recovery rate.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/31-storytelling.html">Chapter 31</a> · <a href="../chapters/32-message-design.html">Chapter 32</a>. <a href="#p05-02">Back to question 2</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="3" data-question="p05-03"><h3>Question 3: D</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Replace the threatening words while preserving the penalty. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Practical freedom remains compromised.</dd>
<dt>B. Keep the implied penalty but add the word voluntary twice. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Labels cannot cancel coercive consequences.</dd>
<dt>C. Count quiet agreement as informed acceptance. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Silence may reflect pressure rather than support.</dd>
<dt>D. Remove refusal penalties and explain the options without pressure. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Both the practical consequences and delivery should support autonomy.</dd>
<dt>E. Offer more promotional stories without explaining refusal. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Stories do not resolve the choice constraint.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/30-persuasion.html">Chapter 30</a> · <a href="../chapters/32-message-design.html">Chapter 32</a>. <a href="#p05-03">Back to question 3</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="2" data-question="p05-04"><h3>Question 4: C</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Treat sympathy as proof that the funding plan is feasible. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Emotional response does not establish feasibility.</dd>
<dt>B. Repeat the story until the funding question is no longer raised. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Repetition avoids the decision-relevant concern.</dd>
<dt>C. Address the funding concern with evidence while retaining the story&#x27;s concrete perspective. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Emotional engagement and the unresolved substantive objection need different support.</dd>
<dt>D. Label the question a lack of empathy. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This treats legitimate scrutiny as a character defect.</dd>
<dt>E. Omit all cost information to preserve the story&#x27;s impact. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>That undermines informed evaluation.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/30-persuasion.html">Chapter 30</a> · <a href="../chapters/31-storytelling.html">Chapter 31</a>. <a href="#p05-04">Back to question 4</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="4" data-question="p05-05"><h3>Question 5: E</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. “The schedule is efficient, so there is no problem.” <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Efficiency does not resolve the relational concern.</dd>
<dt>B. “I know exactly how you feel, so let us move on.” <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Certainty closes the opportunity to correct your understanding.</dd>
<dt>C. “You should use the calendar more carefully.” <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Advice arrives before checking what mattered.</dd>
<dt>D. “Everyone feels that way about schedules.” <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Generalization replaces the colleague&#x27;s specific meaning.</dd>
<dt>E. “Was being excluded the main concern, or have I misunderstood?” <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>A tentative paraphrase invites correction of the inferred concern.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/33-communication.html">Chapter 33</a> · <a href="../chapters/34-connection.html">Chapter 34</a>. <a href="#p05-05">Back to question 5</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="1" data-question="p05-06"><h3>Question 6: B</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. A comprehensive list of forecasting difficulties arranged by data source <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Cataloguing difficulties does not establish which ones can change the choice.</dd>
<dt>B. A demand range and the level at which expansion ceases to be worthwhile <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>These connect the uncertainty to the decision rather than merely acknowledging that estimates may be wrong.</dd>
<dt>C. A general limitations paragraph noting that future conditions may change <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>A general caveat does not show when uncertainty would alter the recommended action.</dd>
<dt>D. A precise central demand estimate accompanied by the authors&#x27; confidence rating <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>A central estimate and confidence rating do not reveal the decision&#x27;s sensitivity to other plausible demand levels.</dd>
<dt>E. A successful expansion elsewhere with a similar estimated average demand <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>A comparison case may be informative but does not locate the relevant decision threshold for this service.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/32-message-design.html">Chapter 32</a> · <a href="../chapters/33-communication.html">Chapter 33</a>. <a href="#p05-06">Back to question 6</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="4" data-question="p05-07"><h3>Question 7: E</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Compare how accurately recipients remember the messages after a week. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Memory is a possible intermediate outcome, not the intended completed behavior.</dd>
<dt>B. Ask a larger sample how likely they would be to share each message. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Sharing intentions need not translate into recipients completing vaccination.</dd>
<dt>C. Repeat the study with a more detailed scale measuring the message&#x27;s credibility. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>More precise credibility measurement does not establish an effect on completed vaccinations.</dd>
<dt>D. Compare recipients&#x27; ratings of the medical expertise conveyed by each message. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Perceived expertise is another judgment about the message, not a direct test of the target behavior.</dd>
<dt>E. Randomly assign the messages in the intended setting and compare completed vaccinations. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>This tests the behavioral outcome the team aims to change rather than treating credibility as an established substitute for it.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/30-persuasion.html">Chapter 30</a> · <a href="../chapters/32-message-design.html">Chapter 32</a>. <a href="#p05-07">Back to question 7</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="3" data-question="p05-08"><h3>Question 8: D</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Ask the team to stop discussing the incident and focus on the next delivery. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Moving attention elsewhere leaves the unfair account in place.</dd>
<dt>B. Privately send the missing instruction and agree on the next handoff date. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This helps the work resume but leaves the public accusation uncorrected.</dd>
<dt>C. Explain privately why the available information originally suggested the colleague was at fault. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Explaining the mistake to the colleague does not repair the public record.</dd>
<dt>D. Correct the account before the same audience and acknowledge the colleague&#x27;s treatment. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Repair should address the false public account and the harm it caused, alongside any operational correction.</dd>
<dt>E. Introduce a checklist that prevents similar omissions in future handoffs. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>A process safeguard does not correct what colleagues were told about this incident.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/33-communication.html">Chapter 33</a> · <a href="../chapters/34-connection.html">Chapter 34</a>. <a href="#p05-08">Back to question 8</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="0" data-question="p05-09"><h3>Question 9: A</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Income doubled afterward; the training&#x27;s causal contribution remains unknown. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Selection and other changes prevent causal attribution from the story alone.</dd>
<dt>B. Training caused this person&#x27;s full income increase. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>No counterfactual isolates that causal contribution.</dd>
<dt>C. Self-selection proves that the training had zero effect. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Failure to identify an effect is not proof of no effect.</dd>
<dt>D. Training doubled income for a typical attendee. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>The selected case does not estimate a typical outcome.</dd>
<dt>E. The case establishes the expected gain for a new applicant. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Transport to new applicants is unsupported.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/31-storytelling.html">Chapter 31</a> · <a href="../chapters/32-message-design.html">Chapter 32</a>. <a href="#p05-09">Back to question 9</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="3" data-question="p05-10"><h3>Question 10: D</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Give staff a simpler explanation of why consistent procedures improve performance. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>The value of consistency does not establish that blocked exceptions are unnecessary.</dd>
<dt>B. Collect more favorable evaluations from staff who mainly handle routine cases. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>These evaluations provide limited evidence about the cases behind the objection.</dd>
<dt>C. Have the pilot&#x27;s strongest advocates demonstrate the routine cases to another team. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Further demonstrations of routine success do not test the problem reported for unusual cases.</dd>
<dt>D. Agree on an exception procedure with staff and test it on the unusual cases. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>This investigates the reported conflict between standardization and professional discretion through a concrete design change.</dd>
<dt>E. Ask an external expert to endorse the workflow before the next implementation meeting. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>An endorsement does not test whether the current boundaries work for unusual cases.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/30-persuasion.html">Chapter 30</a> · <a href="../chapters/33-communication.html">Chapter 33</a> · <a href="../chapters/34-connection.html">Chapter 34</a>. <a href="#p05-10">Back to question 10</a></p></li>
</ol></details></form>

::: {.content-visible when-format="epub"}
Choose one answer (A–E) for each of the 10 questions. Record all your choices before following the link to the answer key. Each question is worth one point.

::: {#p05-01 .practice-question}
**Question 1.** A client accurately summarizes a proposal but declines it. What should the adviser investigate before preparing another explanation?

A) Which communication channel would make the same explanation more familiar
B) Which technical terms need a simpler definition
C) Which visual layout would make the summary easier to scan
D) Which consequences conflict with the client's priorities
E) Which section should be repeated more prominently

:::

::: {#p05-02 .practice-question}
**Question 2.** A presentation opens with a moving patient story and claims that similar patients usually recover after the treatment. Which evidence best supports the frequency claim?

A) The number of favorable treatment stories reported in the local press
B) Clinicians' recollections of the cases they found most striking
C) Follow-up outcomes from a representative sample of comparable patients
D) Satisfaction ratings from patients who completed the full treatment
E) Detailed accounts from several patients selected for successful recovery

:::

::: {#p05-03 .practice-question}
**Question 3.** A manager says a pilot is optional but uses a threatening tone and implies refusal will be remembered. Which redesign best preserves meaningful choice?

A) Replace the threatening words while preserving the penalty.
B) Keep the implied penalty but add the word voluntary twice.
C) Count quiet agreement as informed acceptance.
D) Remove refusal penalties and explain the options without pressure.
E) Offer more promotional stories without explaining refusal.

:::

::: {#p05-04 .practice-question}
**Question 4.** A story increases sympathy for a proposal's beneficiary, but the audience still worries about funding. What is the most useful next step?

A) Treat sympathy as proof that the funding plan is feasible.
B) Repeat the story until the funding question is no longer raised.
C) Address the funding concern with evidence while retaining the story's concrete perspective.
D) Label the question a lack of empathy.
E) Omit all cost information to preserve the story's impact.

:::

::: {#p05-05 .practice-question}
**Question 5.** A colleague says a schedule change made her feel disregarded. Which response best checks understanding before proposing a fix?

A) “The schedule is efficient, so there is no problem.”
B) “I know exactly how you feel, so let us move on.”
C) “You should use the calendar more carefully.”
D) “Everyone feels that way about schedules.”
E) “Was being excluded the main concern, or have I misunderstood?”

:::

::: {#p05-06 .practice-question}
**Question 6.** A policy brief recommends expanding a service. The expansion is worthwhile at high demand but costly at low demand, and future demand is uncertain. Which addition would best help readers assess the recommendation?

A) A comprehensive list of forecasting difficulties arranged by data source
B) A demand range and the level at which expansion ceases to be worthwhile
C) A general limitations paragraph noting that future conditions may change
D) A precise central demand estimate accompanied by the authors' confidence rating
E) A successful expansion elsewhere with a similar estimated average demand

:::

::: {#p05-07 .practice-question}
**Question 7.** A message earns higher credibility ratings in a randomized study. The team is considering using it to increase completed vaccinations. Which follow-up would best test that objective?

A) Compare how accurately recipients remember the messages after a week.
B) Ask a larger sample how likely they would be to share each message.
C) Repeat the study with a more detailed scale measuring the message's credibility.
D) Compare recipients' ratings of the medical expertise conveyed by each message.
E) Randomly assign the messages in the intended setting and compare completed vaccinations.

:::

::: {#p05-08 .practice-question}
**Question 8.** After publicly blaming a colleague for a missed handoff, a manager discovers that an omitted instruction caused the problem. Which response most directly repairs the harm from the accusation?

A) Ask the team to stop discussing the incident and focus on the next delivery.
B) Privately send the missing instruction and agree on the next handoff date.
C) Explain privately why the available information originally suggested the colleague was at fault.
D) Correct the account before the same audience and acknowledge the colleague's treatment.
E) Introduce a checklist that prevents similar omissions in future handoffs.

:::

::: {#p05-09 .practice-question}
**Question 9.** A training advertisement features a top performer whose income doubled after attending. There is no comparison group, and attendees selected themselves. Which revised claim best fits the evidence?

A) Income doubled afterward; the training's causal contribution remains unknown.
B) Training caused this person's full income increase.
C) Self-selection proves that the training had zero effect.
D) Training doubled income for a typical attendee.
E) The case establishes the expected gain for a new applicant.

:::

::: {#p05-10 .practice-question}
**Question 10.** A workflow pilot succeeds on routine cases, but staff report that unusual cases require exceptions the system blocks. A manager proposes a more persuasive presentation before expanding the pilot. Which alternative best tests the substance of the objection?

A) Give staff a simpler explanation of why consistent procedures improve performance.
B) Collect more favorable evaluations from staff who mainly handle routine cases.
C) Have the pilot's strongest advocates demonstrate the routine cases to another team.
D) Agree on an exception procedure with staff and test it on the unusual cases.
E) Ask an external expert to endorse the workflow before the next implementation meeting.

:::

[Finished the set? Check the answers and explanations.](#answers-p05)

::: {#answers-p05 .practice-answer-key}
**Answers and explanations**

Count one point for each correct answer, then review the explanations for any alternatives you considered.

**Question 1: D.**

- **A. Which communication channel would make the same explanation more familiar (Incorrect)** Familiarity with a channel does not identify the client's substantive objection.
- **B. Which technical terms need a simpler definition (Incorrect)** This targets a comprehension problem despite the accurate summary.
- **C. Which visual layout would make the summary easier to scan (Incorrect)** Improved presentation does not directly investigate why an understood proposal was rejected.
- **D. Which consequences conflict with the client's priorities (Correct)** Accurate understanding leaves open substantive disagreement about the proposal's value to the client.
- **E. Which section should be repeated more prominently (Incorrect)** Repetition need not resolve disagreement about consequences.

Review: [Chapter 30](../chapters/30-persuasion.qmd) · [Chapter 33](../chapters/33-communication.qmd). [Back to question 1](#p05-01).

**Question 2: C.**

- **A. The number of favorable treatment stories reported in the local press (Incorrect)** Media selection and an absent patient denominator prevent a recovery-rate estimate.
- **B. Clinicians' recollections of the cases they found most striking (Incorrect)** Memorable cases can be unrepresentative of the patients treated.
- **C. Follow-up outcomes from a representative sample of comparable patients (Correct)** An appropriate sample with outcome follow-up supports an estimate of how frequently recovery occurs; it does not by itself establish a treatment effect.
- **D. Satisfaction ratings from patients who completed the full treatment (Incorrect)** Satisfaction among completers is neither recovery frequency nor a representative outcome measure for all comparable patients.
- **E. Detailed accounts from several patients selected for successful recovery (Incorrect)** Selected successes do not provide the denominator needed to estimate a recovery rate.

Review: [Chapter 31](../chapters/31-storytelling.qmd) · [Chapter 32](../chapters/32-message-design.qmd). [Back to question 2](#p05-02).

**Question 3: D.**

- **A. Replace the threatening words while preserving the penalty. (Incorrect)** Practical freedom remains compromised.
- **B. Keep the implied penalty but add the word voluntary twice. (Incorrect)** Labels cannot cancel coercive consequences.
- **C. Count quiet agreement as informed acceptance. (Incorrect)** Silence may reflect pressure rather than support.
- **D. Remove refusal penalties and explain the options without pressure. (Correct)** Both the practical consequences and delivery should support autonomy.
- **E. Offer more promotional stories without explaining refusal. (Incorrect)** Stories do not resolve the choice constraint.

Review: [Chapter 30](../chapters/30-persuasion.qmd) · [Chapter 32](../chapters/32-message-design.qmd). [Back to question 3](#p05-03).

**Question 4: C.**

- **A. Treat sympathy as proof that the funding plan is feasible. (Incorrect)** Emotional response does not establish feasibility.
- **B. Repeat the story until the funding question is no longer raised. (Incorrect)** Repetition avoids the decision-relevant concern.
- **C. Address the funding concern with evidence while retaining the story's concrete perspective. (Correct)** Emotional engagement and the unresolved substantive objection need different support.
- **D. Label the question a lack of empathy. (Incorrect)** This treats legitimate scrutiny as a character defect.
- **E. Omit all cost information to preserve the story's impact. (Incorrect)** That undermines informed evaluation.

Review: [Chapter 30](../chapters/30-persuasion.qmd) · [Chapter 31](../chapters/31-storytelling.qmd). [Back to question 4](#p05-04).

**Question 5: E.**

- **A. “The schedule is efficient, so there is no problem.” (Incorrect)** Efficiency does not resolve the relational concern.
- **B. “I know exactly how you feel, so let us move on.” (Incorrect)** Certainty closes the opportunity to correct your understanding.
- **C. “You should use the calendar more carefully.” (Incorrect)** Advice arrives before checking what mattered.
- **D. “Everyone feels that way about schedules.” (Incorrect)** Generalization replaces the colleague's specific meaning.
- **E. “Was being excluded the main concern, or have I misunderstood?” (Correct)** A tentative paraphrase invites correction of the inferred concern.

Review: [Chapter 33](../chapters/33-communication.qmd) · [Chapter 34](../chapters/34-connection.qmd). [Back to question 5](#p05-05).

**Question 6: B.**

- **A. A comprehensive list of forecasting difficulties arranged by data source (Incorrect)** Cataloguing difficulties does not establish which ones can change the choice.
- **B. A demand range and the level at which expansion ceases to be worthwhile (Correct)** These connect the uncertainty to the decision rather than merely acknowledging that estimates may be wrong.
- **C. A general limitations paragraph noting that future conditions may change (Incorrect)** A general caveat does not show when uncertainty would alter the recommended action.
- **D. A precise central demand estimate accompanied by the authors' confidence rating (Incorrect)** A central estimate and confidence rating do not reveal the decision's sensitivity to other plausible demand levels.
- **E. A successful expansion elsewhere with a similar estimated average demand (Incorrect)** A comparison case may be informative but does not locate the relevant decision threshold for this service.

Review: [Chapter 32](../chapters/32-message-design.qmd) · [Chapter 33](../chapters/33-communication.qmd). [Back to question 6](#p05-06).

**Question 7: E.**

- **A. Compare how accurately recipients remember the messages after a week. (Incorrect)** Memory is a possible intermediate outcome, not the intended completed behavior.
- **B. Ask a larger sample how likely they would be to share each message. (Incorrect)** Sharing intentions need not translate into recipients completing vaccination.
- **C. Repeat the study with a more detailed scale measuring the message's credibility. (Incorrect)** More precise credibility measurement does not establish an effect on completed vaccinations.
- **D. Compare recipients' ratings of the medical expertise conveyed by each message. (Incorrect)** Perceived expertise is another judgment about the message, not a direct test of the target behavior.
- **E. Randomly assign the messages in the intended setting and compare completed vaccinations. (Correct)** This tests the behavioral outcome the team aims to change rather than treating credibility as an established substitute for it.

Review: [Chapter 30](../chapters/30-persuasion.qmd) · [Chapter 32](../chapters/32-message-design.qmd). [Back to question 7](#p05-07).

**Question 8: D.**

- **A. Ask the team to stop discussing the incident and focus on the next delivery. (Incorrect)** Moving attention elsewhere leaves the unfair account in place.
- **B. Privately send the missing instruction and agree on the next handoff date. (Incorrect)** This helps the work resume but leaves the public accusation uncorrected.
- **C. Explain privately why the available information originally suggested the colleague was at fault. (Incorrect)** Explaining the mistake to the colleague does not repair the public record.
- **D. Correct the account before the same audience and acknowledge the colleague's treatment. (Correct)** Repair should address the false public account and the harm it caused, alongside any operational correction.
- **E. Introduce a checklist that prevents similar omissions in future handoffs. (Incorrect)** A process safeguard does not correct what colleagues were told about this incident.

Review: [Chapter 33](../chapters/33-communication.qmd) · [Chapter 34](../chapters/34-connection.qmd). [Back to question 8](#p05-08).

**Question 9: A.**

- **A. Income doubled afterward; the training's causal contribution remains unknown. (Correct)** Selection and other changes prevent causal attribution from the story alone.
- **B. Training caused this person's full income increase. (Incorrect)** No counterfactual isolates that causal contribution.
- **C. Self-selection proves that the training had zero effect. (Incorrect)** Failure to identify an effect is not proof of no effect.
- **D. Training doubled income for a typical attendee. (Incorrect)** The selected case does not estimate a typical outcome.
- **E. The case establishes the expected gain for a new applicant. (Incorrect)** Transport to new applicants is unsupported.

Review: [Chapter 31](../chapters/31-storytelling.qmd) · [Chapter 32](../chapters/32-message-design.qmd). [Back to question 9](#p05-09).

**Question 10: D.**

- **A. Give staff a simpler explanation of why consistent procedures improve performance. (Incorrect)** The value of consistency does not establish that blocked exceptions are unnecessary.
- **B. Collect more favorable evaluations from staff who mainly handle routine cases. (Incorrect)** These evaluations provide limited evidence about the cases behind the objection.
- **C. Have the pilot's strongest advocates demonstrate the routine cases to another team. (Incorrect)** Further demonstrations of routine success do not test the problem reported for unusual cases.
- **D. Agree on an exception procedure with staff and test it on the unusual cases. (Correct)** This investigates the reported conflict between standardization and professional discretion through a concrete design change.
- **E. Ask an external expert to endorse the workflow before the next implementation meeting. (Incorrect)** An endorsement does not test whether the current boundaries work for unusual cases.

Review: [Chapter 30](../chapters/30-persuasion.qmd) · [Chapter 33](../chapters/33-communication.qmd) · [Chapter 34](../chapters/34-connection.qmd). [Back to question 10](#p05-10).

:::
